title: TCP and UDP
about: Two ways to send data: careful and in order, or fast with no promises.

cards.prompt:
**TCP** is a tracked parcel: lost pieces are resent and put back in order. **UDP** is a postcard: quick, nothing checked or resent, so it suits **live** things, where late data is useless.

Which suits each job?

items.label: Saving a document to the cloud
Your car's position in a racing game

cards.explanation: Downloads, email, photos and saved files break if one piece is missing, so they use **TCP**. Calls, voice chat and game positions are about **right now**, so they usually use **UDP**: waiting would only cause lag.
cards.hint: Would one missing piece ruin it, or is it live, so old data is useless?
cards.nudge: By the time a lost bit of a call or game could be resent, a newer one has replaced it.

cards.title: Reliable or fast
cards.body:
**TCP** (Transmission Control [[Protocol]]) is the parcel: it sets up a connection, numbers the pieces so they go back in order, and resends anything lost.

**UDP** (User Datagram Protocol) is the postcard: no setup, no checks. Quick, but lost data stays lost.

Both travel inside IP [[packets|packet]] and use **ports**.

cards.prompt:
Before sending data, TCP checks both sides can hear each other with three messages: the **three-way handshake**.

Put them in order.

items.label: Browser asks for the web page

cards.explanation: The browser asks (**SYN**, *synchronise*), the server agrees and checks back (**SYN-ACK**), and the browser confirms (**ACK**, *acknowledge*). Only then does the request go.
cards.hint: Each message answers the one before, and no data goes until all three are done.
cards.nudge: The request waits for the handshake: which message starts it, and which replies to a question?

cards.prompt: On a video call, one [[packet]] goes missing. If the call used **TCP**, what would happen?

options.text: The picture freezes until it's resent, then jumps
The call skips the lost piece and carries on
options.nudge: Skipping is what a postcard does: what does the tracked parcel insist on?

options.text: The call ends, since TCP can't cope with a gap
options.nudge: TCP doesn't give up after one lost piece: what does it do with missing data?

options.text: The call quietly switches to UDP instead
options.nudge: TCP never turns into another protocol: it has its own way to handle a lost piece.

cards.explanation: TCP waits for the lost piece to be **resent** and keeps everything in order, so the picture freezes, then catches up. That's why calls usually use **UDP**.
cards.hint: TCP resends and keeps order: what must the video do while it waits?

cards.prompt: Match each activity to the reason it's delivered that way.

pairs.right: Every piece must arrive, in order

pairs.left: Voice chat in a game (usually UDP)
pairs.right: Fresh sound matters more than late sound
One tiny question, not worth a setup

cards.explanation: A download needs every piece (**TCP**), and voice chat would rather skip a lost moment (**UDP**). A DNS lookup is so small a handshake would take longer, so it usually uses **UDP**, switching to TCP for large answers.
cards.hint: Ruined by one missing piece, better off skipping old data, or too small for a setup?
cards.nudge: Think tracked parcel versus postcard, and how small a DNS question is next to a [[handshake]].

options.text: It sends with no handshake and never resends
No resending, but it always delivers in order
options.nudge: Putting data back in order is TCP's job: UDP makes no promises.

options.text: It travels on its own, outside IP packets
options.nudge: Both TCP and UDP travel inside IP packets.

options.text: It skips ports, so it serves one program at a time
options.nudge: Both need to reach the right program on a computer: what does that job?

cards.explanation: UDP has **no handshake**, **no resending** and no promise of order. Like [[TCP]], it travels inside IP packets and uses ports; [[DNS]] lookups are a common example.
cards.hint: UDP is the postcard: which statement fits that and nothing more?

cards.prompt: Your browser sends a SYN, but the server's SYN-ACK reply is **lost** on the way. What happens?

options.text: Both sides wait, then resend their message
It opens anyway, since the server got the SYN
options.nudge: The connection needs all three steps, and the browser never heard back.

options.text: The browser sends data without finishing
options.nudge: TCP never sends data before the handshake: what does a side do when no reply comes?

options.text: The browser automatically switches to UDP
options.nudge: TCP doesn't turn into another protocol: it has its own way to handle lost messages.

cards.explanation: The browser never got a SYN-ACK, so it **resends its SYN**; the server never got an ACK, so it **resends its SYN-ACK**. Once all three get through the connection opens, and after several failures the browser shows an error.
cards.hint: The connection opens only after all three arrive: what is each side still waiting for?

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- **TCP**: a handshake first, numbered pieces, and resending anything lost.
- **UDP**: no handshake, no resending; quick, but lost data stays lost.
- Files and email need TCP; live calls and games prefer UDP.

Next: the rules on top, like [[HTTP]], DNS and email.
